title: My Daily Brief
overview: This edition is dominated by the US midterm elections: turnout, Election Day glitches, what control of Congress could mean, and how the Iran war is affecting Republicans. Binance released its account of the record crypto theft that the FBI attributes to North Korea. Also covered: a hoax-letter arrest, an Asian Cup postponement, South Korea's Olympic bid, Apple policy changes and a fatal crash in Rock Hill.

stories.headline: Binance says fake job interviews and an internal AI tool enabled record crypto theft
stories.summary: Binance published a postmortem on Tuesday describing how attackers stole roughly $6.3–6.4 billion from the exchange in what outlets call the largest crypto theft to date. The company said the multi-stage campaign began in June, when an engineer downloaded a tampered installer for an AI tool. It continued in September, when a second engineer was lured through fake job interviews into running malicious code on his work computer. The attackers then abused an internal AI tool and stolen credentials and launched the theft on October 29. The FBI has attributed the attack to a North Korean unit called TraderTraitor, and Binance says customers will not bear the losses.
key_facts: The FBI attributed the theft to a North Korean state-linked unit known as TraderTraitor.
Binance says the intrusion began in June 2026 and the theft was launched on October 29 between 17:15 and 19:56.
CEO Richard Teng said 98% of affected tokens have been replenished and the rest are being procured; about $2.85 billion has been frozen or intercepted.
Teng told Fox Business that "this should not have happened" and that the company bears full responsibility.
Binance says it has rebuilt affected systems and commissioned an independent cybersecurity review.

perspectives.framing: NPR told the story through the engineer who thought he was job-hunting and quoted Binance's apology. The Verge reported the technical details but questioned why such a well-known tactic still worked, and noted how little Binance disclosed about the internal AI tool.

The Hacker News gave a detailed technical timeline drawn from Binance's report. Axios framed the theft as part of a wider North Korean strategy of exploiting both sides of the job market. The Hill gave a brief summary.
Fox Business centered on the interview with Teng, stressing that customers lose nothing, Binance's large reserves, and a return to normal operations.

disputed: Outlets give different totals: The Hacker News says $6.43 billion, others say $6.3 billion, and Fox says more than $6 billion.
Binance has given few details about the internal AI tool and why it could be misused.
The Verge reports the first malware spread through a malicious Google ad; Binance's account as quoted refers only to a search engine.
The timeline relies largely on Binance's own account.
stories.why: It shows how social engineering combined with AI tools can lead to theft on an unprecedented scale, with implications for any company whose staff are job-hunting online.

stories.headline: Americans vote in midterms that will decide control of Congress
stories.summary: Voters cast ballots on Tuesday to decide control of the House and Senate, both currently held by Republicans. Polls and oddsmakers cited by several outlets favored Democrats to win the House, while the Senate was expected to be close. Analysts say a Democratic win in either chamber would sharply limit President Trump's agenda and give Democrats subpoena power. Some outlets also examined how the result could shape US policy on Ukraine and Iran. Final results could take days or weeks in some races.
key_facts: Democrats need to flip four Senate seats and three House seats to win control.
Key Senate contests include Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas.
The BBC reports Trump's approval rating at around 37%.
On Election Day, ICE posted on X: "If you vote illegally, we will find you."

perspectives.framing: PBS/AP live updates highlighted ICE's warning to voters, quoted an election expert who called it unfortunate, and noted that noncitizen voting is rare. Al Jazeera and The Guardian framed the vote as a check on Trump's power.
CNBC focused on gridlock and market reaction scenarios, citing Stifel analysts. DW examined the foreign policy stakes for Ukraine and Iran. The BBC featured voters' views of Trump.

disputed: Which party will control the Senate was considered too close to call.
How quickly results will be known, especially in Alaska.
stories.why: The outcome determines how much resistance Trump faces in Congress for his final two years.

stories.headline: Strong turnout reported across states, including the Carolinas
stories.summary: Election officials in several states, including North Carolina, Georgia, Michigan and Florida, reported strong turnout on Election Day after record early voting. In the Carolinas, closely watched races include the North Carolina Senate contest between Democrat Roy Cooper and Republican Michael Whatley, and the South Carolina governor's race. North Carolina results will not be posted until at least 8:15 p.m. because some precincts extended their hours.
key_facts: More than 2.8 million early ballots were cast in North Carolina.
More than 1 million South Carolinians voted early, over 80% more than in 2022.
Georgia had recorded 775,000 Election Day votes by afternoon, with about 1.4 million expected.
Florida reported more than 1.86 million Election Day votes by afternoon.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian's live blog highlighted surging turnout and profiled voters, including Minneapolis residents leaving stickers at memorials for people killed by immigration officers and a Republican veteran in Alaska.
WSOC provided practical local coverage: poll hours, precinct extensions and the main Carolina races.
The Washington Examiner published a neutral guide to when polls close in each state.

stories.why: High turnout and the timing of results shape how quickly control of Congress will be known.

stories.headline: Iran war weighs on Republicans in midterms, outlets report
stories.summary: Several outlets examined how the US-Israeli war on Iran, launched in February, is affecting the midterms. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis called it a "big, big drag" on Republicans because of higher gas prices. Reason reported that several GOP Senate candidates distanced themselves from the war late in their campaigns after earlier supporting it. DW quoted analysts who said a Democratic Congress would have limited power to change Iran policy and that the two parties broadly agree on Iran. The Washington Examiner, citing Reuters, reported that Iran has dragged out negotiations to deny Trump a pre-election win.
key_facts: DeSantis called the Iran war a "big, big drag" on Republican candidates.
Rep. Ashley Hinson voted six times against measures to limit the war before saying in September that Iowans shouldn't "foot the bill."
A Change Research poll found a plurality of military families and veterans oppose the war.
Trump can veto congressional limits on the war, and overriding a veto requires two-thirds of both chambers.

perspectives.framing: DW emphasized the limits on what Congress can do and a bipartisan consensus on Iran, quoting John Bolton and Iran experts. The Hill reported DeSantis's remarks.

Right-leaning outlets were split. Reason (libertarian) and the Daily Caller sharply criticized the war and Republicans' reluctance to acknowledge its costs, with the Daily Caller comparing it to Biden-era inflation messaging. The Washington Examiner focused on Iran trying to influence the election and argued the strategy could backfire.

disputed: Reports that the US and Israel are preparing new strikes after the election are unconfirmed.
Trump's claim that only "one or two targets" remain in Iran.
Iran's motives for prolonging talks, as reported by Reuters and interpreted by analysts.
stories.why: The war's cost and its effect on prices may influence both the election result and what Congress does about the war afterward.

stories.headline: Oklahoma man charged over hundreds of white-powder letters sent before elections
stories.summary: Federal authorities charged Oklahoma City resident Robin Martin with conveying a hoax and mailing threatening communications. He is accused of sending more than 700 letters containing white powder to election officials, members of Congress, pollsters, media and law enforcement ahead of the 2024 and 2026 elections. The powders tested so far were flour or yeast, though not all letters have been tested. Martin was arrested Monday and was expected in federal court in Oklahoma City on Tuesday.
key_facts: The letters' return address read "U.S.T.E.A., United States Traitor Elimination Army."
The letters warned of arrests for treason and, according to an FBI affidavit, claimed Trump won the 2020 election.
The FBI cites video of Martin's car at mailboxes and his fingerprints on a letter addressed to FBI Director Kash Patel.
The mailings led to evacuations of election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma.

perspectives.framing: PBS/AP gave a detailed account of the evidence and included the affidavit's description of the letters' 2020 election claims.
The Hill gave a brief factual summary of the charges.
The Washington Examiner stressed that the recipients were bipartisan and placed the case among recent hoax-letter incidents. It did not mention the letters' claims about the 2020 election.

disputed: Not all letters have been tested.
Martin had no attorney listed and has not responded to the charges publicly.
stories.why: The case shows the threats and disruption facing election officials during voting periods.

stories.headline: Woman, 37, killed by pickup truck while crossing Cherry Road in Rock Hill
stories.summary: A 37-year-old woman died Monday evening after a pickup truck hit her as she crossed Cherry Road in Rock Hill, South Carolina. Police said she was crossing outside a crosswalk while wearing dark clothing. The driver stayed at the scene, no charges have been filed, and police are investigating. A separate report covered an 84-year-old pedestrian killed on McConnells Highway in York County on Sunday.
key_facts: The crash happened Monday, Nov. 2, near Oakland Avenue in the 500 block of Cherry Road.
The victim died at the scene and has not been identified.
No charges have been filed.

perspectives.framing: Local TV stations reported the police account in nearly identical terms.

disputed: Reports give the time as either about 6:20 p.m. or 6:30 p.m.
stories.why: It is the second fatal pedestrian crash reported in York County in two days.

stories.headline: Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia postponed to December 2027 after Houthi attacks
stories.summary: The Asian Football Confederation moved the Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia from Jan. 7–Feb. 5, 2027, to Dec. 23, 2027–Jan. 21, 2028. It cited logistical complexities and travel disruptions in the region. The decision follows Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including a deadly strike on Riyadh's airport. The new dates still need FIFA approval.
key_facts: CNA reports the October strike on Riyadh's airport killed 13 people and closed it for about two weeks.
The tournament features 24 teams at venues in Riyadh, Jeddah and Khobar.
South Korea's players' union had pushed for the postponement.
Saudi organizers say they are "fully ready" for the new dates.

perspectives.framing: Korean outlets focused on the uncertainty for caretaker coach Robert Moreno and the Korea Football Association's leadership vacuum. Singapore's CNA focused on its team's preparations. DW placed the move in the context of security problems and Saudi Arabia scaling back its sports spending.

disputed: FIFA has not yet approved the new dates.
Moreno's future as South Korea's coach is uncertain.
stories.why: Regional conflict is disrupting major sporting events and calling into question Saudi Arabia's role as a host.

stories.headline: Technical problems delay some voting and results in NC, NY and Georgia
stories.summary: North Carolina extended voting at several polling places that opened late because of computer and printer problems, which delays the release of statewide results. In New York's Westchester County, voting machines could not scan ballots, which were set aside to be counted later. Scanner malfunctions in Georgia's Fulton County affected 1,069 early ballots. Officials said the glitches were routine and not malicious.
key_facts: NC elections director Sam Hayes said disruptions "are not indications of malicious activity."
Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins called the scanning problem "completely unacceptable" and promised a review.
Fulton County proposed a different counting process for 1,069 early ballots after two scanners malfunctioned.

perspectives.framing: WFAE gave a short factual report on the North Carolina extensions, noting that officials said the problems were resolved and backups were used.

The Washington Examiner covered several states and highlighted that the affected areas lie in competitive districts. It noted Republican concerns that the Westchester problem could advantage the Democratic challenger, while also quoting officials who said the issues were not malicious.

disputed: Reports differ on the affected NC counties: WFAE lists Hertford, Wilson, Lenoir and Columbus, while the Examiner lists Hertford, Gates, Lenoir and Wilson.
Reports differ on when NC results will be released: at least 8:15 p.m. (WFAE, WSOC) or 8:30 p.m. (Examiner).
stories.why: Glitches in close districts can delay results and fuel disputes over the count.

stories.headline: Apple sets 18+ rating for dating and AI companion apps and opens Siri AI to third-party apps
stories.summary: Apple told developers that apps with dating or romantic features, including AI companions with sexual or romantic content, must carry an 18+ rating, with new content descriptors required from November 16. Apps that share users' real-world locations must also disclose it. Separately, Apple's iOS 27.3 developer preview lets developers integrate Siri AI into all apps, allowing it to carry out tasks using personal context and what is on screen.
key_facts: The new age-rating descriptors take effect November 16.
Top AI companion apps had been downloaded 220 million times as of last summer.
Siri AI's expanded features are also coming to Apple's own apps, including Mail, Maps and Messages.

perspectives.framing: The Verge covered the Siri expansion as a product feature, using Apple's own examples.
TechCrunch framed the age-rating change around child safety and its possible effect on AI companion apps aimed at younger users.

disputed: How strictly the rules will apply to apps where companion features are only one part of the app.
stories.why: The changes affect what minors can access on iPhones and how much the AI assistant can do inside apps.

stories.headline: South Korea named among seven candidates for 2036 Summer Olympics
stories.summary: The IOC finalized seven potential hosts for the 2036 Summer Games: South Korea, Germany, Hungary, India, Qatar, South Africa and Turkey. South Korea's candidate, North Jeolla Province, is moving toward co-hosting with Seoul because it lacks enough infrastructure on its own. The national Olympic committee and the sports ministry pledged full support and urged the two sides to reach a deal quickly.
key_facts: Candidates will give virtual presentations to the IOC this month.
The IOC Executive Board will open "strategic dialogue" with candidates in March 2027.
South Korea hosted the 1988 Summer and 2018 Winter Olympics.

perspectives.framing: Yonhap (also carried by The Korea Herald) reported official statements of support and the unresolved co-hosting talks.

disputed: North Jeolla and Seoul have not yet agreed on co-hosting.
stories.why: It sets the timeline for South Korea's bid to host a third Olympics.
